extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, patent agents, and practitioners dealing with U.S. specification requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the three separate requirements that a patent specification must satisfy under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph): written description, enablement (manner and process of making and using), and best mode, including the required quality of disclosure and case law distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must include a written description of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory wording: the specification 'shall contain a written description of the invention.' Case law (Ariad Pharm. v. Eli Lilly; Vas‑Cath v. Mahurkar; Vasudevan Software v. MicroStrategy; In re Barker) establishes that the written description requirement is distinct from enablement. Examples/notes: An invention may be described without the disclosure being enabling (e.g., a chemical compound disclosed without a method of making it). The presence of some discussion showing possession of claimed subject matter can create genuine issues of fact as to written description support (see Vasudevan Software example concerning 'disparate databases').

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (manner and process of making and using the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose the manner and process of making and using the invention in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory wording: disclosure must be 'in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains... to make and use the same.' Enablement is a separate requirement from written description (Ariad; Vas‑Cath). Examples/notes: A disclosure can be enabling without adequately describing the invention (e.g., a method of making and using a paint composition with functionally defined ingredients might enable formulations that fall within the description but not describe any specific formulation). Conversely, a description may exist but lack an apparent or disclosed method of making it (e.g., a chemical compound lacking a synthetic method). Case law emphasizes separate factual inquiries for enablement versus written description (see Vasudevan Software, In re Armbruster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory wording: the specification 'shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor... of carrying out the invention.' The best mode requirement is distinct from enablement (see In re Newton). Guidance: the inventor must disclose the preferable way they contemplated practicing the invention at the time of filing; failure to do so can implicate best mode (subject to statutory changes and enforcement practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of disclosure: 'full, clear, concise, and exact' terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification's disclosure must meet the quality standard of being full, clear, concise, and exact so as to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrase appears in both 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph and sets an express sufficiency standard applied to the manner/process (enablement) and, by practice, to disclosure generally. Examiners and courts evaluate whether the disclosure meets these qualitative terms when assessing enablement and related sufficiency issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: The three requirements are separate and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description, enablement, and best mode are separate, distinct requirements that must each be considered independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court holdings (Ariad en banc; Vas‑Cath; In re Barker) affirm that Congress intended separate requirements and that one requirement (e.g., enablement) does not subsume the others. Practical effect: an application may satisfy one requirement but fail another; examiners and courts must analyze each requirement on its own factual and legal basis. The MPEP gives examples illustrating separability (e.g., descriptive but non‑enabling disclosures, enabling but non‑descriptive disclosures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability by filing date: AIA (35 U.S.C. 112(a)) vs pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Which statutory provision applies depends on the application's filing date: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) applies to applications filed on or after September 16, 2012; pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph applies to earlier applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP quotes both the post‑AIA 112(a) and the pre‑AIA 112 first paragraph language; practitioners must apply the correct statutory text and interpretive framework depending on filing date. Although the core three requirements appear in both texts, citations and procedural practice may differ by era.
